pathway.title: MOLINA HEALTHCARE, INC. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: The first finding is the speed of the earnings decline. Operating income fell from USD 1,707 million in FY2024 to USD 781 million in FY2025 and to a calculated USD 172 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, while debt stayed near USD 3,771 million, so calculated EBITDA of USD 1,893 million, USD 976 million and USD 333 million puts total debt at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x [CP-1 financials table]. The mechanism is a fixed premium rate set against a medical cost trend that outran it: the medical care ratio was 89.1% in FY2024, 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in nine months 2026, and the implied fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss of USD 162 million [CP-1 calculations]. Because debt did not fall, each point of margin lost translates directly into higher leverage. On the parent cash basis net debt is 9.50x EBITDA for the same twelve months. This is a calculated, Documentary Fact finding with high confidence in the inputs and medium confidence in the EBITDA definition, since the company reports no EBITDA.

The second finding is that covenant headroom, the question that matters most for creditors, cannot be measured. The credit agreement requires minimum interest coverage, which the February 4, 2026 amendment reduced from 3.0 to 1.0 to 1.75 to 1.00 through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters, and a maximum debt to capital ratio of 60%; the company states compliance at September 30, 2026 [CP-1 observations]. A simple EBITDA over interest expense measure is 1.56x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, or 2.00x with the USD 93 million non-cash impairment added back, but the agreement defines the ratio and that definition and the reported ratio are not supplied. The mechanism is that relief was taken in advance and the floor rises as the amendment expires; the implication is that earnings must recover materially during 2027 or relief must be extended, and a simple-basis shortfall is illustrated under Calculations. Confidence is low because the decisive figure is absent.

The third finding is that liquidity is adequate for debt service but sits at the parent. Consolidated cash and cash equivalents were USD 4,479 million at September 30, 2026, yet most of it supports claims and statutory capital at regulated health plans; parent cash and investments were USD 608 million against USD 223 million at December 31, 2025, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn, and no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028 [CP-1 liquidity and maturity tables]. Subsidiary dividends to the parent were USD 985 million in 2025 and the parent received USD 329 million of dividends and return of capital in nine months 2026, against an expected decline in dividends payable without approval [CP-1 observations]. The mechanism is that creditors rely on subsidiary distributions that fall when earnings fall and that the parent must fund statutory capital first, so the revolver is the real backstop; letters of credit drawn on it are not printed, so availability net of letters of credit is unconfirmed.

The fourth finding is the maturity and refinancing profile. The five senior notes total USD 3,800 million in principal: USD 800 million in 2028, USD 650 million in 2030, USD 850 million in 2031, USD 750 million in 2032 and USD 750 million in 2033, at an annual coupon of about USD 191.4 million, or 5.04% of principal. Recent issuance priced at 6.500% in November 2025 and 6.250% in November 2024, so any refinancing at current levels raises cost, while LTM interest expense of USD 213 million already consumes a large share of the USD 333 million of EBITDA. The implication is limited near-term refinancing pressure but little capacity to absorb a further earnings shock before 2028.

The fifth finding concerns business risk. Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue and four state contracts (California, New York, Texas and Washington) are about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue [CP-1A operating model]. Medicaid contracts run three to five years and either party may terminate, so re-procurement outcomes and annual rate setting drive revenue, and the Virginia contract loss shows the exposure. Management states that 2026 is the trough year for Medicaid margins and that recent rate updates are strong for 2027, which is Management Language that the results through the third quarter of 2026 do not yet support: the Medicaid medical care ratio was 93.0% in the third quarter against 92.0%. The sixth finding is that near-term earnings carry identified drags: guidance includes a loss of USD 1.50 per diluted share from the new Florida contract and a loss of USD 1.00 per diluted share from the Medicare product to be exited for 2027, and the GAAP guidance floor of USD 122 million net income implies only about USD 10 million for the fourth quarter. The sources conflict on the scale of the Florida contract (about 120,000 enrollees against USD 6 billion of annual premium revenue), so the size of that start-up cost cannot be verified [CP-1A conflicts].

The seventh finding is capital allocation and governance. The company repurchased USD 1,000 million of stock in FY2025, paused repurchases in nine months 2026 and retains USD 500 million of authorization through December 31, 2026, which is an Analyst Interpretation of Neutral or Mixed behaviour: the pause is supportive, but the authorization is a possible call on parent cash. The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 and the derivative dismissal notice was filed on October 6, 2026, which removes an overhang. The only rating evidence is BB from S&P and Ba2 from Moody's as stated in the annual report.

runs.text: Strengths. The first strength is a favourable maturity and liquidity structure: no principal is due before USD 800 million in June 2028, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn and runs to November 20, 2030, and parent cash and investments rose to USD 608 million from USD 223 million, so the debt can be serviced for some time even on thin earnings (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The second is an unsecured, single-issuer capital structure at the parent with no sponsor, no creditor-adverse transaction found and no dividend recapitalisation, which limits governance and structural-priming risk (Documentary Fact, CP-1A, with the caveat that indentures are not supplied). The third is an established government-programme franchise with recent state procurement wins and a large Medicaid base; the contract win record is a management claim and is tagged Management Language, but the wins themselves are documented (CP-1A). The fourth is the pause in share repurchases in nine months 2026 and the dismissal of the securities and derivative suits, which reduce competing calls on parent cash and a legal overhang (Documentary Fact, CP-1 and CP-1A). The fifth is that operating cash flow was positive in nine months 2026 at USD 629 million, giving an operating cash flow less capital expenditure figure of USD 535 million, although this reflects settlement timing (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1).

Weaknesses. The first weakness is leverage on collapsed earnings: 11.32x total debt to EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026 against 1.54x in FY2024, with a simple EBITDA over interest expense of 1.56x (Documentary Fact for inputs, calculated, CP-1). The second is unverifiable covenant headroom against a floor that rises from 1.75 to 1.00 to 2.75 to 1.00 by September 2027 (Insufficient Information on the executed definition and ratio; the relief obtained in advance is an Analyst Interpretation of limited headroom). The third is dependence on subsidiary dividends and on consolidated cash that is largely tied to statutory capital, so the headline net cash position does not measure parent debt-service capacity (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1). The fourth is concentration in Medicaid and in four states, with short and terminable contracts and an unproven margin recovery (Documentary Fact and Management Language, CP-1A). The fifth is settlement-driven cash flow: operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 535 million in FY2025 and an inflow of USD 629 million in nine months 2026, so cash conversion is volatile (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The sixth is the identified 2026 and 2027 earnings drags from the Florida start-up and the Medicare exit, together with policy risk from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with the Florida contract size in conflict across the sources (Documentary Fact and conflict, CP-1A).

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: There is no leveraged buyout, sponsor transaction or pending merger in the sources, and no financing transaction after the February 4, 2026 credit agreement amendment appears in the pinned sources up to the cutoff; the transaction history is organic growth through state procurements plus bolt-on acquisitions and refinancings. Status of each item below is as stated in the sources.

New debt and facilities (Documentary Fact, status: completed). On November 20, 2025 the company completed a private offering of $850 million of 6.500% senior notes due February 15, 2031, with interest payable semiannually on February 15 and August 15 from August 15, 2026 and deferred issuance costs of $12 million; net proceeds repaid $740 million of term loan debt under the prior credit agreement and funded general corporate purposes (10-K page:131). The same day the company entered a new credit agreement replacing the June 8, 2020 agreement, with a $1.25 billion revolver terminating November 20, 2030, a $15 million swingline, a $100 million letter-of-credit sub-facility and uncommitted incremental term loans of up to $800 million for acquisitions (10-K page:131); Truist Bank is administrative agent (10-K page:153). Earlier, $750 million of 6.250% notes due January 15, 2033 were issued in November 2024 (10-K pages 83, 130). The February 4, 2026 First Amendment temporarily reduced the minimum interest coverage ratio to 1.75 to 1.00 for quarters through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters (10-K page:132); the amendment was agreed before the Q1 2026 reporting and is a subsequent event relative to the FY2025 balance sheet. During 2025 the company borrowed 950 of term loans and 150 under the credit facility and repaid all of them (10-K page:132). Liquidity effect: the notes refinanced the term loans and left the revolver undrawn; parent cash and investments are in CP-1. Use of proceeds, amounts and rates are stated in the filing; the executed indentures and credit agreement are not in the pinned set, so covenant baskets and restricted-payment capacity are Insufficient Information.

Acquisitions (Documentary Fact, status: completed). ConnectiCare Holding Company, Inc., "a wholly owned subsidiary of EmblemHealth, Inc.", was acquired effective February 1, 2025 for $350 million, serving about 140,000 members across Marketplace, Medicare and certain commercial products (10-K page:12); it is 4% of total assets and 4% of revenues in FY2025 and was excluded from the internal control assessment (10-K page:146). The 2024 Bright acquisition used $295 million of net cash (10-K page:92). The sources state that acquisition appetite remains ("we remain opportunistic about deploying capital to accretive acquisitions", Management Language, 10-K page:10), but the incremental term loan is uncommitted and no acquisition is announced; no inference is drawn from one deal.

Shareholder distributions (Documentary Fact). The company purchased about 1,679,000 shares for $500 million in Q1 2025 (average $297.83) and about 2,849,000 shares for $500 million in Q3 2025 (average $175.50) (10-K page:13); it made no purchases under the program in 9M 2026, and $500 million remained available through December 31, 2026 as of October 16, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:40). Subsidiary dividends to the parent were 985 in 2025 (10-K page:90).

Subsequent events to the cutoff (Documentary Fact). The new Florida Kids Medicaid contract commenced on October 1, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:29); the securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 and the plaintiff filed a dismissal of the derivative action on October 6, 2026 (10-Q Q3 pages 18-19); the Q3 release dated October 21, 2026 reaffirmed FY2026 guidance (Q3 release page:2). Nothing dated after the cutoff is used.

fields.value: The financial base is well supported for reported facts and weaker for derived credit metrics. Reported facts: Molina is a managed-care payer whose earnings compressed sharply as the medical care ratio (MCR, medical costs over premium revenue) rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026, so that operating income fell from 1,707 in FY2024 to 781 in FY2025 and to 334 in 9M 2026 against 943 in 9M 2025. Debt is five parent-level senior unsecured notes with 3,800 of principal and 3,771 of carrying value at September 30, 2026, no amount drawn on the 1,250 revolver, and no principal due before June 2028. Calculated metrics, not reported by the company: EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization) was 1,893 in FY2024, 976 in FY2025 and 333 for the LTM to September 30, 2026, which puts total debt to EBITDA at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x. The mechanism is operating leverage on a fixed debt stack: debt did not fall while earnings did, and interest expense rose from 118 in FY2024 to 192 in FY2025 after the November 2024 and November 2025 note issuances and the 2025 term loan borrowings. Interest expense over the LTM to September 30, 2026 was 213, so EBITDA over interest expense is 1.56x on this simple basis, below the 1.75 to 1.00 covenant floor in force through December 31, 2026. That comparison is not a covenant test: the credit agreement defines the ratio and the sources do not print the definition or the reported ratio, the company states it is in compliance (10-Q Q3 page:15), and adding back the 93 non-cash impairment alone lifts the simple ratio to 2.00x. The consolidated balance sheet shows net cash (consolidated cash and equivalents of 4,479 exceed debt of 3,771), but most of that cash supports claims and statutory capital at the regulated health plans, so the parent view (608 of cash and investments) is the better liquidity guide for debt service. Near-term maturity pressure is limited because no principal falls due before June 2028, so the credit question is earnings recovery and covenant headroom rather than refinancing in the next year. What the evidence supports: the reported statements, debt table, maturities, revolver size and parent cash. What it restricts: any statement of covenant headroom, cash-interest coverage for the latest twelve months, or revolver availability net of letters of credit. The context holds no ratings, so the only rating evidence is the annual report sentence that each senior note is rated BB by S&P and Ba2 by Moody's (10-K page:94).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a listed, sponsor-free managed-care organisation that "provides managed healthcare services under the Medicaid and Medicare programs, and through the state insurance marketplaces" (10-K, page:108), operating in 21 states with about 4.9 million members at September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3, page:5). Its customers are government payers ("Our primary customers are state Medicaid agencies and the federal government", 10-Q Q3, page:31), so revenue is a fixed per-member-per-month premium that the health plan underwrites against medical cost, and the credit mechanism is the gap between rate updates (set annually by states and CMS) and medical cost trend. That gap is the central fact of the period: the 10-K describes a "rate and trend imbalance that we believe to be temporary" (page:86), the medical care ratio rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026 (CP-1), and earnings compressed accordingly (CP-1 operating income, EBITDA and leverage). The business is concentrated: Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue (page:15), four state contracts (California, New York, Texas, Washington) each exceed 10% of Medicaid premium revenue, and Medicaid contracts run three to five years with either side able to terminate with or without cause (page:108), so each re-procurement is a revenue-durability event (Virginia was lost: contracts terminated June 30, 2025, page:12). Two portfolio actions are reshaping 2026 and 2027: the Marketplace book is being cut deliberately (9M 2026 Marketplace premium revenue 1,994 against 3,401, membership 267,000 against 713,000, 10-Q Q3 pages 31-34) and the traditional Medicare Advantage-Part D product will be exited for 2027 with a 93 impairment recognized in Q1 2026 (CP-1). Management's long-term growth targets (premium revenue growth of 11% to 13% and passing $50 billion in 2027, 10-K page:10) are Management Language and sit against FY2026 premium revenue guidance of approximately $42 billion, so they are not used as a base case. No sponsor, controlling holder, dividend recapitalisation or related-party leakage appears in the sources; the documented capital-allocation behaviour is a pattern of share repurchases funded by subsidiary dividends, assessed below as Neutral or Mixed. Debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes plus an undrawn revolver (CP-1); whether subsidiaries guarantee the notes is not stated in the sources. The evidence supports a business and transaction read at the level of Documentary Facts; it restricts conclusions on ownership, control rights and covenant capacity because the proxy-based ownership information and executed documents are not supplied.

fields.value: New debt and facilities (Documentary Fact, status: completed). On November 20, 2025 the company completed a private offering of $850 million of 6.500% senior notes due February 15, 2031, with interest payable semiannually on February 15 and August 15 from August 15, 2026 and deferred issuance costs of $12 million; net proceeds repaid $740 million of term loan debt under the prior credit agreement and funded general corporate purposes (10-K page:131). The same day the company entered a new credit agreement replacing the June 8, 2020 agreement, with a $1.25 billion revolver terminating November 20, 2030, a $15 million swingline, a $100 million letter-of-credit sub-facility and uncommitted incremental term loans of up to $800 million for acquisitions (10-K page:131); Truist Bank is administrative agent (10-K page:153). Earlier, $750 million of 6.250% notes due January 15, 2033 were issued in November 2024 (10-K pages 83, 130). The February 4, 2026 First Amendment temporarily reduced the minimum interest coverage ratio to 1.75 to 1.00 for quarters through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters (10-K page:132); the amendment was agreed before the Q1 2026 reporting and is a subsequent event relative to the FY2025 balance sheet. During 2025 the company borrowed 950 of term loans and 150 under the credit facility and repaid all of them (10-K page:132). Liquidity effect: the notes refinanced the term loans and left the revolver undrawn; parent cash and investments are in CP-1. Use of proceeds, amounts and rates are stated in the filing; the executed indentures and credit agreement are not in the pinned set, so covenant baskets and restricted-payment capacity are Insufficient Information.

fields.value: Acquisitions (Documentary Fact, status: completed). ConnectiCare Holding Company, Inc., "a wholly owned subsidiary of EmblemHealth, Inc.", was acquired effective February 1, 2025 for $350 million, serving about 140,000 members across Marketplace, Medicare and certain commercial products (10-K page:12); it is 4% of total assets and 4% of revenues in FY2025 and was excluded from the internal control assessment (10-K page:146). The 2024 Bright acquisition used $295 million of net cash (10-K page:92). The sources state that acquisition appetite remains ("we remain opportunistic about deploying capital to accretive acquisitions", Management Language, 10-K page:10), but the incremental term loan is uncommitted and no acquisition is announced; no inference is drawn from one deal.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: As of 2026-11-05, this credit snapshot gives the fundamental credit view of MOLINA HEALTHCARE, INC. It synthesises the financial base and the business and transaction fact pack from the upstream modules only, in USD, for Q3 2026 against FY2025 and FY2024. It gives no peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The context file (sha256 038deefd3d0187dee809d7ec7eb3f32548cc8a768b8a64a8e4dfbffc4bec802f) holds run settings only; its ratings, sponsor, guarantor and deal-term fields are blank and are not treated as zero.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a deteriorating credit with adequate near-term liquidity: debt of USD 3,771 million equals 11.32x EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against 1.54x in FY2024 [CP-1 leverage table]. The strongest support is structure and timing: the debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes, no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028, and the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn. The weakest point is earnings: the medical care ratio reached 92.1% in nine months 2026 against 90.8%, leaving LTM EBITDA of USD 333 million against interest expense of USD 213 million. The outcome depends on whether Medicaid rate updates restore margins before the interest coverage floor steps up in 2027, which the sources cannot confirm.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The first finding is the speed of the earnings decline. Operating income fell from USD 1,707 million in FY2024 to USD 781 million in FY2025 and to a calculated USD 172 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, while debt stayed near USD 3,771 million, so calculated EBITDA of USD 1,893 million, USD 976 million and USD 333 million puts total debt at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x [CP-1 financials table]. The mechanism is a fixed premium rate set against a medical cost trend that outran it: the medical care ratio was 89.1% in FY2024, 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in nine months 2026, and the implied fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss of USD 162 million [CP-1 calculations]. Because debt did not fall, each point of margin lost translates directly into higher leverage. On the parent cash basis net debt is 9.50x EBITDA for the same twelve months. This is a calculated, Documentary Fact finding with high confidence in the inputs and medium confidence in the EBITDA definition, since the company reports no EBITDA.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The second finding is that covenant headroom, the question that matters most for creditors, cannot be measured. The credit agreement requires minimum interest coverage, which the February 4, 2026 amendment reduced from 3.0 to 1.0 to 1.75 to 1.00 through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters, and a maximum debt to capital ratio of 60%; the company states compliance at September 30, 2026 [CP-1 observations]. A simple EBITDA over interest expense measure is 1.56x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, or 2.00x with the USD 93 million non-cash impairment added back, but the agreement defines the ratio and that definition and the reported ratio are not supplied. The mechanism is that relief was taken in advance and the floor rises as the amendment expires; the implication is that earnings must recover materially during 2027 or relief must be extended, and a simple-basis shortfall is illustrated under Calculations. Confidence is low because the decisive figure is absent.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The third finding is that liquidity is adequate for debt service but sits at the parent. Consolidated cash and cash equivalents were USD 4,479 million at September 30, 2026, yet most of it supports claims and statutory capital at regulated health plans; parent cash and investments were USD 608 million against USD 223 million at December 31, 2025, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn, and no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028 [CP-1 liquidity and maturity tables]. Subsidiary dividends to the parent were USD 985 million in 2025 and the parent received USD 329 million of dividends and return of capital in nine months 2026, against an expected decline in dividends payable without approval [CP-1 observations]. The mechanism is that creditors rely on subsidiary distributions that fall when earnings fall and that the parent must fund statutory capital first, so the revolver is the real backstop; letters of credit drawn on it are not printed, so availability net of letters of credit is unconfirmed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The fourth finding is the maturity and refinancing profile. The five senior notes total USD 3,800 million in principal: USD 800 million in 2028, USD 650 million in 2030, USD 850 million in 2031, USD 750 million in 2032 and USD 750 million in 2033, at an annual coupon of about USD 191.4 million, or 5.04% of principal. Recent issuance priced at 6.500% in November 2025 and 6.250% in November 2024, so any refinancing at current levels raises cost, while LTM interest expense of USD 213 million already consumes a large share of the USD 333 million of EBITDA. The implication is limited near-term refinancing pressure but little capacity to absorb a further earnings shock before 2028.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The fifth finding concerns business risk. Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue and four state contracts (California, New York, Texas and Washington) are about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue [CP-1A operating model]. Medicaid contracts run three to five years and either party may terminate, so re-procurement outcomes and annual rate setting drive revenue, and the Virginia contract loss shows the exposure. Management states that 2026 is the trough year for Medicaid margins and that recent rate updates are strong for 2027, which is Management Language that the results through the third quarter of 2026 do not yet support: the Medicaid medical care ratio was 93.0% in the third quarter against 92.0%. The sixth finding is that near-term earnings carry identified drags: guidance includes a loss of USD 1.50 per diluted share from the new Florida contract and a loss of USD 1.00 per diluted share from the Medicare product to be exited for 2027, and the GAAP guidance floor of USD 122 million net income implies only about USD 10 million for the fourth quarter. The sources conflict on the scale of the Florida contract (about 120,000 enrollees against USD 6 billion of annual premium revenue), so the size of that start-up cost cannot be verified [CP-1A conflicts].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The seventh finding is capital allocation and governance. The company repurchased USD 1,000 million of stock in FY2025, paused repurchases in nine months 2026 and retains USD 500 million of authorization through December 31, 2026, which is an Analyst Interpretation of Neutral or Mixed behaviour: the pause is supportive, but the authorization is a possible call on parent cash. The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 and the derivative dismissal notice was filed on October 6, 2026, which removes an overhang. The only rating evidence is BB from S&P and Ba2 from Moody's as stated in the annual report.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. The first strength is a favourable maturity and liquidity structure: no principal is due before USD 800 million in June 2028, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn and runs to November 20, 2030, and parent cash and investments rose to USD 608 million from USD 223 million, so the debt can be serviced for some time even on thin earnings (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The second is an unsecured, single-issuer capital structure at the parent with no sponsor, no creditor-adverse transaction found and no dividend recapitalisation, which limits governance and structural-priming risk (Documentary Fact, CP-1A, with the caveat that indentures are not supplied). The third is an established government-programme franchise with recent state procurement wins and a large Medicaid base; the contract win record is a management claim and is tagged Management Language, but the wins themselves are documented (CP-1A). The fourth is the pause in share repurchases in nine months 2026 and the dismissal of the securities and derivative suits, which reduce competing calls on parent cash and a legal overhang (Documentary Fact, CP-1 and CP-1A). The fifth is that operating cash flow was positive in nine months 2026 at USD 629 million, giving an operating cash flow less capital expenditure figure of USD 535 million, although this reflects settlement timing (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. The first weakness is leverage on collapsed earnings: 11.32x total debt to EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026 against 1.54x in FY2024, with a simple EBITDA over interest expense of 1.56x (Documentary Fact for inputs, calculated, CP-1). The second is unverifiable covenant headroom against a floor that rises from 1.75 to 1.00 to 2.75 to 1.00 by September 2027 (Insufficient Information on the executed definition and ratio; the relief obtained in advance is an Analyst Interpretation of limited headroom). The third is dependence on subsidiary dividends and on consolidated cash that is largely tied to statutory capital, so the headline net cash position does not measure parent debt-service capacity (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1). The fourth is concentration in Medicaid and in four states, with short and terminable contracts and an unproven margin recovery (Documentary Fact and Management Language, CP-1A). The fifth is settlement-driven cash flow: operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 535 million in FY2025 and an inflow of USD 629 million in nine months 2026, so cash conversion is volatile (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The sixth is the identified 2026 and 2027 earnings drags from the Florida start-up and the Medicare exit, together with policy risk from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with the Florida contract size in conflict across the sources (Documentary Fact and conflict, CP-1A).
